# Direction Angle of a 2D Vector in Terms of Arctangent

## Statement

Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity embedded in a Cartesian plane $P$, expressed in component form as
$$\mathbf a = x\,\mathbf i + y\,\mathbf j , \qquad x, y \in \mathbb R .$$
Let $\theta$ denote the direction of $\mathbf a$, measured from the positive direction of the $x$-axis and taken (by the usual convention) in the half-open interval $(-\pi, \pi]$. Then
$$\theta = \begin{cases}
\arctan\!\left(\dfrac y x\right) & : x > 0 \\[2pt]
\arctan\!\left(\dfrac y x\right) + \pi & : x < 0 \text{ and } y \ge 0 \\[2pt]
\arctan\!\left(\dfrac y x\right) - \pi & : x < 0 \text{ and } y < 0 \\[2pt]
\dfrac \pi 2 & : x = 0 \text{ and } y > 0 \\[2pt]
-\dfrac \pi 2 & : x = 0 \text{ and } y < 0 \\[2pt]
\text{undefined} & : x = 0 \text{ and } y = 0
\end{cases}$$
where $\arctan$ is the real arctangent function, i.e. the inverse of the restriction of $\tan$ to $\left(-\tfrac\pi2, \tfrac\pi2\right)$.

**The claim is true as stated.** A complete proof follows.

---

## 0. Conventions, and the precise meaning of "direction"

Write
$$r := \left|\mathbf a\right| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$$
for the magnitude of $\mathbf a$.

The direction of a non-zero plane vector $\mathbf a$ is the angle through which the positive $x$-axis must be rotated about the origin (anticlockwise counted positive) to bring it into the direction of $\mathbf a$. Rotating the unit vector $\mathbf i$ anticlockwise through an angle $\theta$ carries it to $\cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j$, so the vector of magnitude $r$ pointing in that direction is $r\cos\theta\,\mathbf i + r\sin\theta\,\mathbf j$. Hence, in analytic form, the assertion "$\theta$ is the direction of $\mathbf a$" is exactly the pair of equations

$$x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta \tag{$*$}$$

together with the normalising convention $\theta \in (-\pi,\pi]$. (Some normalisation is indispensable: rotations through $\theta$ and through $\theta + 2k\pi$, $k \in \mathbb Z$, have the same effect, so without it $\theta$ would be determined only modulo $2\pi$. The interval $(-\pi,\pi]$ is the convention fixed in the statement.)

Accordingly, we work with the following precise definition.

> **Definition.** Let $\mathbf a = x\,\mathbf i + y\,\mathbf j \ne \mathbf 0$ and $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. The **direction** of $\mathbf a$ is the unique $\theta \in (-\pi,\pi]$ satisfying $(*)$.

Lemma 1 below shows that such a $\theta$ exists and is unique, so this definition is legitimate; Lemma 1 also shows that for $\mathbf a = \mathbf 0$ uniqueness fails as badly as possible, which is the content of the last line of the statement.

The facts about the real trigonometric functions that will be used are the standard ones, listed here for reference:

* **(T1)** $\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$ for all $t \in \mathbb R$.
* **(T2)** $\cos$ is continuous and strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, with $\cos 0 = 1$, $\cos\frac\pi2 = 0$ and $\cos\pi = -1$; $\sin t \ge 0$ for $t \in [0,\pi]$, with $\sin 0 = \sin\pi = 0$ and $\sin\frac\pi2 = 1$; and $\cos t > 0$ for $t \in \left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$.
* **(T3)** $\cos$ is even and $\sin$ is odd: $\cos(-t) = \cos t$, $\sin(-t) = -\sin t$.
* **(T4)** $\cos(s-t) = \cos s\cos t + \sin s \sin t$ for all $s,t \in \mathbb R$.
* **(T5)** $\cos u = 1$ if and only if $u \in 2\pi\mathbb Z$.
* **(T6)** $\cos(t \pm \pi) = -\cos t$ and $\sin(t \pm \pi) = -\sin t$ for all $t \in \mathbb R$.
* **(T7)** $\tan := \frac{\sin}{\cos}$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$ with image $\mathbb R$. Hence $\arctan : \mathbb R \to \left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$ is a well-defined, strictly increasing bijection satisfying $\tan(\arctan t) = t$ for all $t \in \mathbb R$. In particular $\arctan 0 = 0$, and by strict monotonicity
  $$t > 0 \implies \arctan t > 0, \qquad t = 0 \implies \arctan t = 0, \qquad t < 0 \implies \arctan t < 0. \tag{T7$'$}$$

---

## 1. Lemma 1 (Existence and uniqueness of the direction)

**Lemma 1.** Let $(x,y) \in \mathbb R^2$ and let $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$.

**(a)** If $(x,y) \neq (0,0)$, then there is exactly one $\theta \in (-\pi,\pi]$ satisfying $(*)$.

**(b)** If $(x,y) = (0,0)$, then *every* $\theta \in \mathbb R$ satisfies $(*)$.

### Proof of (b)

If $x = y = 0$ then $r = 0$, and $(*)$ reads $0 = 0\cdot\cos\theta$ and $0 = 0\cdot\sin\theta$, both of which hold for every real $\theta$. $\square$

### Proof of (a): existence

Suppose $(x,y) \ne (0,0)$. Then $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} > 0$, so $(*)$ is equivalent to
$$\cos\theta = \frac x r, \qquad \sin\theta = \frac y r . \tag{$**$}$$
Since $x^2 \le x^2 + y^2 = r^2$, we have $\left|\frac x r\right| \le 1$, i.e. $\frac x r \in [-1,1]$.

By (T2), $\cos$ restricted to $[0,\pi]$ is continuous and strictly decreasing with $\cos 0 = 1$, $\cos\pi = -1$; by the Intermediate Value Theorem its image contains $[-1,1]$, by (T1) its image is contained in $[-1,1]$, and strict monotonicity makes it injective. Hence
$$\cos\big|_{[0,\pi]} : [0,\pi] \longrightarrow [-1,1]$$
is a bijection. Let $\phi \in [0,\pi]$ be the unique number with $\cos\phi = \dfrac x r$. Since $\sin\phi \ge 0$ on $[0,\pi]$ (T2), (T1) gives
$$\sin\phi = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2\phi} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{x^2}{r^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{r^2 - x^2}{r^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{y^2}{r^2}} = \frac{\left|y\right|}{r} .$$

*Case $y \ge 0$.* Then $\left|y\right| = y$, so $\theta := \phi$ satisfies $\cos\theta = \frac x r$ and $\sin\theta = \frac y r$, and $\theta \in [0,\pi] \subseteq (-\pi,\pi]$.

*Case $y < 0$.* Then $\sin\phi = \frac{\left|y\right|}{r} > 0$, so $\phi \notin \{0,\pi\}$ (because $\sin 0 = \sin\pi = 0$), i.e. $\phi \in (0,\pi)$. Put $\theta := -\phi \in (-\pi,0) \subseteq (-\pi,\pi]$. By (T3),
$$\cos\theta = \cos\phi = \frac x r, \qquad \sin\theta = -\sin\phi = -\frac{\left|y\right|}{r} = \frac y r ,$$
the last equality because $y<0$ gives $\left|y\right| = -y$.

In either case a $\theta \in (-\pi,\pi]$ satisfying $(**)$, hence $(*)$, has been exhibited. $\square$

### Proof of (a): uniqueness

Let $\theta_1,\theta_2 \in (-\pi,\pi]$ both satisfy $(**)$. By (T4),
$$\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2) = \cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + \sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2 = \frac x r\cdot\frac x r + \frac y r\cdot\frac y r = \frac{x^2+y^2}{r^2} = 1 .$$
By (T5), $\theta_1 - \theta_2 = 2k\pi$ for some $k \in \mathbb Z$. But $\theta_1,\theta_2 \in (-\pi,\pi]$ forces $\theta_1 - \theta_2 \in (-2\pi, 2\pi)$, so $\left|2k\pi\right| < 2\pi$, whence $k = 0$ and $\theta_1 = \theta_2$. $\blacksquare$

### Consequence: the case $x = y = 0$

By Lemma 1(b), when $x = y = 0$ *every* real number satisfies the defining equations $(*)$. No angle is singled out, so $\mathbf a = \mathbf 0$ has no well-defined direction: $\theta$ is undefined. (Equivalently and more elementarily: the zero vector points nowhere. Note also that the expression $\arctan\frac y x$ occurring in the other branches is itself undefined here, since $\frac 0 0$ is undefined — so no branch of the formula could have been used.) **This proves the sixth case of the theorem.**

---

## 2. Lemma 2 (Sine and cosine of $\arctan\frac y x$)

**Lemma 2.** Let $x,y \in \mathbb R$ with $x \ne 0$, let $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and set $\alpha := \arctan\!\left(\dfrac y x\right)$. Then $\alpha$ is defined, $\alpha \in \left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$, and
$$\cos\alpha = \frac{\left|x\right|}{r} > 0, \qquad \sin\alpha = \frac y x \cdot \frac{\left|x\right|}{r} .$$
Explicitly:
$$x > 0 \implies \big(\cos\alpha,\ \sin\alpha\big) = \left(\frac x r,\ \frac y r\right), \qquad x < 0 \implies \big(\cos\alpha,\ \sin\alpha\big) = \left(-\frac x r,\ -\frac y r\right) .$$

### Proof

Since $x \ne 0$, the quotient $\frac y x$ is defined, so $\alpha = \arctan\frac y x$ is defined; and $r^2 = x^2 + y^2 \ge x^2 > 0$ gives $r \ge \left|x\right| > 0$, so all quotients below make sense.

By (T7), $\alpha \in \left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$ and $\tan\alpha = \dfrac y x$. By (T2), $\cos\alpha > 0$; in particular $\cos\alpha \ne 0$, so $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha}$ and, dividing (T1) (at $t = \alpha$) by $\cos^2\alpha$,
$$1 + \tan^2\alpha = \frac{1}{\cos^2\alpha} .$$
Substituting $\tan\alpha = \frac y x$,
$$\frac{1}{\cos^2\alpha} = 1 + \frac{y^2}{x^2} = \frac{x^2+y^2}{x^2} = \frac{r^2}{x^2},$$
so $\cos^2\alpha = \dfrac{x^2}{r^2}$ and therefore $\left|\cos\alpha\right| = \dfrac{\left|x\right|}{r}$. Since $\cos\alpha > 0$,
$$\cos\alpha = \frac{\left|x\right|}{r},$$
and consequently
$$\sin\alpha = \tan\alpha\,\cos\alpha = \frac y x \cdot \frac{\left|x\right|}{r} .$$

If $x > 0$ then $\left|x\right| = x$, so $\cos\alpha = \dfrac x r$ and $\sin\alpha = \dfrac y x\cdot\dfrac x r = \dfrac y r$.

If $x < 0$ then $\left|x\right| = -x$, so $\cos\alpha = -\dfrac x r$ and $\sin\alpha = \dfrac y x\cdot\dfrac{-x}{r} = -\dfrac y r$. $\blacksquare$

---

## 3. Proof of the theorem

The six listed cases are mutually exclusive and exhaustive: exactly one of $x>0$, $x<0$, $x=0$ holds; in the case $x<0$ exactly one of $y \ge 0$, $y<0$ holds; and in the case $x = 0$ exactly one of $y>0$, $y<0$, $y=0$ holds.

The case $x = y = 0$ was settled at the end of §1. In each of the five remaining cases $(x,y) \ne (0,0)$, hence $r > 0$, and by Lemma 1(a) the direction $\theta$ is the **unique** element of $(-\pi,\pi]$ satisfying $(**)$. So in each case it suffices to:

1. name the candidate value $\theta_0$ given by the statement;
2. verify $\theta_0 \in (-\pi,\pi]$;
3. verify $\cos\theta_0 = \dfrac x r$ and $\sin\theta_0 = \dfrac y r$;

for then the uniqueness clause of Lemma 1(a) gives $\theta = \theta_0$, which is the assertion of that branch.

### Case 1: $x > 0$

Put $\alpha := \arctan\dfrac y x$ and $\theta_0 := \alpha$.

*Range.* By (T7), $\theta_0 = \alpha \in \left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right) \subseteq (-\pi,\pi]$.

*Equations.* By Lemma 2 in the case $x>0$: $\cos\theta_0 = \dfrac x r$ and $\sin\theta_0 = \dfrac y r$.

Hence $\theta = \arctan\dfrac y x$, as claimed.

### Case 2: $x < 0$ and $y \ge 0$

Put $\alpha := \arctan\dfrac y x$ and $\theta_0 := \alpha + \pi$.

*Range.* From $x<0$ and $y \ge 0$ we get $\dfrac y x \le 0$, so by (T7$'$) $\alpha \le 0$; and $\alpha > -\frac\pi2$ by (T7). Thus $\alpha \in \left(-\frac\pi2,\,0\right]$ and
$$\theta_0 = \alpha + \pi \in \left(\tfrac\pi2,\ \pi\right] \subseteq (-\pi,\pi] .$$
(The boundary sub-case $y=0$ gives $\alpha = \arctan 0 = 0$ and $\theta_0 = \pi$, which indeed lies in $(-\pi,\pi]$ — this is why the interval is closed at $\pi$.)

*Equations.* By Lemma 2 in the case $x<0$: $\cos\alpha = -\dfrac x r$ and $\sin\alpha = -\dfrac y r$. Hence by (T6),
$$\cos\theta_0 = \cos(\alpha+\pi) = -\cos\alpha = \frac x r, \qquad \sin\theta_0 = \sin(\alpha+\pi) = -\sin\alpha = \frac y r .$$

Hence $\theta = \arctan\dfrac y x + \pi$, as claimed.

### Case 3: $x < 0$ and $y < 0$

Put $\alpha := \arctan\dfrac y x$ and $\theta_0 := \alpha - \pi$.

*Range.* From $x<0$ and $y<0$ we get $\dfrac y x > 0$, so by (T7$'$) $\alpha > 0$; and $\alpha < \frac\pi2$ by (T7). Thus $\alpha \in \left(0,\tfrac\pi2\right)$ and
$$\theta_0 = \alpha - \pi \in \left(-\pi,\ -\tfrac\pi2\right) \subseteq (-\pi,\pi] .$$

*Equations.* By Lemma 2 in the case $x<0$: $\cos\alpha = -\dfrac x r$ and $\sin\alpha = -\dfrac y r$. Hence by (T6),
$$\cos\theta_0 = \cos(\alpha-\pi) = -\cos\alpha = \frac x r, \qquad \sin\theta_0 = \sin(\alpha-\pi) = -\sin\alpha = \frac y r .$$

Hence $\theta = \arctan\dfrac y x - \pi$, as claimed.

### Case 4: $x = 0$ and $y > 0$

Here $r = \sqrt{0^2 + y^2} = \left|y\right| = y > 0$. Put $\theta_0 := \dfrac\pi2 \in (-\pi,\pi]$. By (T2),
$$\cos\theta_0 = \cos\frac\pi2 = 0 = \frac 0 r = \frac x r, \qquad \sin\theta_0 = \sin\frac\pi2 = 1 = \frac y y = \frac y r .$$
Hence $\theta = \dfrac\pi2$, as claimed.

### Case 5: $x = 0$ and $y < 0$

Here $r = \sqrt{0^2+y^2} = \left|y\right| = -y > 0$. Put $\theta_0 := -\dfrac\pi2 \in (-\pi,\pi]$. By (T3) and (T2),
$$\cos\theta_0 = \cos\!\left(-\frac\pi2\right) = \cos\frac\pi2 = 0 = \frac x r, \qquad \sin\theta_0 = \sin\!\left(-\frac\pi2\right) = -\sin\frac\pi2 = -1 = \frac{y}{-y} = \frac y r .$$
Hence $\theta = -\dfrac\pi2$, as claimed.

### Case 6: $x = 0$ and $y = 0$

Proved at the end of §1: $\mathbf a = \mathbf 0$ has no well-defined direction, so $\theta$ is undefined.

All six cases having been treated, the theorem is proved. $\blacksquare$

---

## 4. Remarks (consistency checks)

**(1) The branches respect the convention and partition $(-\pi,\pi]$.** The values produced by the five defined branches are:

| region | value of $\theta$ | geometric meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x>0$ | $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$ | open right half-plane |
| $x<0,\ y\ge 0$ | $\left(\frac\pi2,\pi\right]$ | second quadrant, plus the negative $x$-axis ($\theta=\pi$) |
| $x<0,\ y<0$ | $\left(-\pi,-\frac\pi2\right)$ | third quadrant |
| $x=0,\ y>0$ | $\frac\pi2$ | positive $y$-axis |
| $x=0,\ y<0$ | $-\frac\pi2$ | negative $y$-axis |

These five sets of angles are pairwise disjoint and their union is
$$\left(-\pi,-\tfrac\pi2\right) \cup \left\{-\tfrac\pi2\right\} \cup \left(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right) \cup \left\{\tfrac\pi2\right\} \cup \left(\tfrac\pi2,\pi\right] = (-\pi,\pi] ,$$
as it must be, since by Lemma 1 the direction map $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\} \to (-\pi,\pi]$ is surjective (every $\theta \in (-\pi,\pi]$ is the direction of $\cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j$).

**(2) The shifts by $\pm\pi$ are forced, not arbitrary.** For $x<0$ the naive value $\arctan\frac y x$ lies in $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$ and so has positive cosine, contradicting the requirement $\cos\theta = \frac x r < 0$; by Lemma 2 it is in fact the direction of $-\mathbf a$. Adding $\pi$ reverses the pointing and so corrects this. One must then subtract a further $2\pi$ — i.e. subtract $\pi$ rather than add it — exactly when $\arctan\frac y x + \pi > \pi$, i.e. when $\arctan\frac y x > 0$, i.e. by (T7$'$) when $\frac y x > 0$, i.e. (given $x<0$) when $y<0$. That is precisely the split between Cases 2 and 3.

**(3) Discontinuity across the negative $x$-axis.** For $x<0$ fixed, letting $y \uparrow 0^{-}$ gives $\theta \to -\pi$, whereas at $y = 0$ the value is $\theta = \pi$. This jump of $2\pi$ is unavoidable for *any* single-valued choice of direction angle on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{\mathbf 0\}$, and is not a defect of this particular formula.
